transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-15
Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Park (Redwood AE), Riley Chen (Redwood SE), Alex Morgan (CTO, Polaris), Priya Singh (Lead Engineer), Samir Patel (DevOps)
Recording: yes

Summary: Quick SDK walkthrough focusing on getting Polaris devs up and running with Redwood's Python/TypeScript SDKs, auth patterns, env setup, and private deployment considerations. Action items and security docs to be shared.

[00:00:00] Jamie: All right welcome everyone, thanks for taking the time. Uh quick intro — I'm Jamie, AE at Redwood, and with me is Riley our solutions engineer. How are you all doing today?
[00:00:12] Alex: Good thanks. Morning from New York. Excited to see the SDK and how fast we can get something in dev.
[00:00:18] Priya: Hi, yep thanks team. We want to try both python and typescript examples, and get an idea of networking and KMS constraints.
[00:00:28] Riley: Awesome. We'll walk through the quickstart repo (github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-quickstart — shared in chat) and run a live example. We'll also cover auth: API key flow for dev and SSO/machine identity for production, and then touch on hosted vs private deployment tradeoffs.

[00:02:05] Riley: Ok first slide high-level — the SDK wraps the REST API and supports streaming, function calling, embeddings. In python it's pip install redwood, typescript via npm @redwood/inference. Example code is minimal: set REDWOOD_API_KEY env var and call client.generate.
[00:02:40] Priya: Quick question — for local dev do we need to run docker or can we just pip install and call the hosted endpoint?
[00:02:48] Riley: You can do either. For quick iteration use the hosted endpoint with an API key. If you want local offline tests there's a docker image we provide but it's mostly for private deployments.

[00:04:12] Jamie: We'll drop the quickstart link and a minimal snippet in the follow-up email — it's the same snippet we demo here.

[00:05:00] [Live demo begins - Riley sharing screen] 
[00:05:10] Riley: I'm in the python quickstart. Step one: pip install redwood-inference. Step two: export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk_live_xxx or set it in a .env. Step three run python examples/generate.py.
[00:05:34] Alex: Does the API key need any special roles?
[00:05:40] Riley: Good call — keys can be scoped. For dev just a basic key works; for production we recommend role-scoped service keys and short-lived tokens (we integrate with SSO and can mint ephemeral tokens via OIDC).
[00:06:05] Priya: How does SSO work for machine-to-machine? We use Okta and need automatic rotation.
[00:06:11] Riley: We support OIDC and can integrate with Okta to mint ephemeral credentials using a service account. We'll share the integration guide. There's also KMS integration for encrypting keys at rest — you can bring your own KMS (AWS KMS, Google KMS, Azure Key Vault).

[00:08:00] Riley: Now switching to the TypeScript quickstart. npm i @redwood/inference, create a client new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }), and then await client.chat.create({ model: 'rwd-small', messages: [...] }) — streaming is supported via events or callbacks.
[00:08:42] Samir: Any SDK differences regarding batching or rate limit handling between py/ts?
[00:08:50] Riley: Same semantics; the SDK exposes helpers: automatic retry, backoff, and batching helpers. For high throughput we recommend server-side continuous batching or use our dedicated endpoints which expose a batching config.

[00:10:20] Alex: For our use case — chat summaries across support tickets — latency matters but so does cost. Do you have recommended defaults?
[00:10:30] Jamie: Typical pattern: small model for embeddings + mid-size for summarization; enable prefix KV caching to reduce token costs; choose dedicated for predictable p99 latency. We can provide default config tuned for short prompt lengths like yours.

[00:12:05] Riley: I'm going to show env setup in the repo — .env.example includes REDWOOD_API_KEY, REDWOOD_REGION, REDWOOD_MODEL, and optional REDWOOD_KMS_PROVIDER. We also have a docker-compose for local testing that mocks the network.
[00:12:40] Priya: Can we pin model versions in the SDK call? We need deterministic outputs for our audits.
[00:12:47] Riley: Yes, you can pass model_version: "rwd-2026-05-01" in the call to pin. Also the console supports rollout pins and can freeze a model for a given route.

[00:14:18] Alex: Security — do you persist logs or transcripts by default? We need strict retention policies.
[00:14:25] Riley: By default hosted API keeps minimal logs for debugging; enterprise customers get configurable retention and audit logs. With Private you control retention and logs are routed to your syslog/S3. We'll share the security whitepaper.

[00:16:02] Riley: Now quick network note: For VPC/private deployments, egress IPs are provided for allowlist, and there is a peering option. If you use Dedicated you can also use private endpoints — depends on whether you want fully isolated compute.
[00:16:30] Samir: We run strict egress rules so we'll need the exact IP ranges. Also curious about TLS mTLS support?
[00:16:40] Riley: We support mTLS for private endpoints and can provision certs or accept your certs. We'll include sample nginx/proxy config in the checklist.

[00:18:50] Jamie: Quick note on costs: hosted per-token pricing, dedicated reserved capacity pricing, and private licenses. For initial POC most customers do hosted with a monthly cap and then move to dedicated when they need p99 guarantees.

[00:21:05] Priya: For devs, what's a minimal integration timeline? We have 2 engineers who can pick this up next week.
[00:21:12] Riley: Minimal: 1-2 dev days to wire up client and basic calls, plus a day to run integration tests. If you want SSO+KMS and VPC it's more like 1-2 weeks of ops work. We can provide a template repo and CI example.

[00:23:40] Riley: Demo: running python generate shows streaming tokens coming back. Note: transcript shows small transcription artifact where the SDK prints "K V cache" instead of "KV cache" — minor doc wording we'll fix.
[00:24:15] Alex: Ha, ok. Important we get consistent naming for docs.

[00:25:50] Riley: I'm going to show the console briefly — route configuration, pinning, and cost per token breakdown. You can create API keys with role scoping and attach them to a route.
[00:26:20] Priya: Can we create keys scoped to a single model and to a specific set of endpoints?
[00:26:24] Riley: Yep, scope by model, by route, and by quota. Also you can limit token spend per key which is handy for dev/test accounts.

[00:28:00] Alex: About logs and evals — can we run quality monitors against a set of prompts?
[00:28:06] Jamie: Redwood Optimize has evals and regression alerts. You upload test prompt sets and monitor quality regressions when changing models or quantization. We'll include an example prompt set.

[00:30:15] Samir: On the private side — how does KMS integration work for encrypting cache and model weights?
[00:30:24] Riley: We encrypt keys and prefixes using your KMS; model weights aren't typically encrypted at rest in our hosted offering, but in private deployments we can provide disk-level encryption and HSM options. We'll forward a matrix of supported providers.

[00:32:40] Priya: Any gotchas with TypeScript SSR serverless lambdas? We run on Vercel/Netlify for some parts.
[00:32:47] Riley: For serverless cold starts you may want to reuse warm clients and avoid reloading heavy model artifacts; use streaming or chunking to reduce latency. We have a serverless example showing how to reuse the client across invocations.

[00:34:55] Alex: For our benchmark request — we plan to run 100 concurrent chat sessions of short prompts. Will that map cleanly to your dedicated config?
[00:35:05] Riley: Yes, we'll propose a dedicated pool config. For 100 concurrent short sessions we typically recommend X GPUs (we'll put exact GPU counts in the benchmarking doc) and a batching config with max tokens per request tuned to your median length. We'll schedule a bench run.

[00:37:12] Priya: About logs — we also need audit logs to go to our SIEM. Is that supported?
[00:37:18] Riley: Yes, audit logs can be shipped to your S3 or Splunk/Datadog. Private deployments can keep logs entirely inside your VPC.

[00:39:30] Jamie: Ok recap — we'll send the quickstart repo, the VPC checklist and security whitepaper, and a proposed benchmark plan. Priya will send network egress IPs and KMS provider. Samir will confirm whether dedicated is an option.

[00:40:05] Alex: Sounds good. Any preliminary pricing ranges you can share right now?
[00:40:12] Jamie: For hosted POC it's typical to see monthly spend in the low thousands for moderate volume; dedicated commitments vary by GPU type — we'll send a pricing sheet with bucketed examples.

[00:42:20] Priya: Can you also include example terraform for private deployment? We manage infra as code.
[00:42:27] Riley: Yep we have terraform modules and a terraform example for private / on-prem bootstrapping. Will attach.

[00:44:40] [Quick Q&A wrap]
[00:44:45] Samir: One last infra nit — do you support bring-your-own-licensing for certain model engines?
[00:44:52] Riley: We can support customer-owned model binaries in Private deployments; on Hosted we curate models but we also bring your models behind dedicated/private.

[00:46:10] Jamie: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the benchmark session.
[00:46:20] Alex: Thanks, talk soon.
[00:46:24] Priya: Thanks all.
[00:46:30] [call ends]
